detail.abstract: This paper seeks to examine the historiographical construction of the Second World War, focusing on the dichotomy between the "Victors' Narrative" and the socio-political reality of the German State (1933-1945). By employing a comparative framework, the study investigates why certain imperialistic atrocities of the mid-20th century were integrated into the "progress of civilization," while the German model was uniquely externalized as an absolute moral anomaly. The paper analyzes the linguistic shift from "State-centric" to "Ideology-centric" terminology and explores the implications of prolonged postwar propaganda on contemporary historical objectivity.

title: The Relationship Between Agricultural Technology Adoption and Rural Poverty: Evidence from Survey-Based Analysis

detail.title: The Relationship Between Agricultural Technology Adoption and Rural Poverty: Evidence from Survey-Based Analysis
detail.abstract: This study examines the influence of agricultural technology adoption on rural poverty, with particular emphasis on adoption rates, socioeconomic impacts, and incentives for rural households. While agricultural technology can affect rural households in diverse ways, adoption rates vary significantly across socioeconomic groups. Primary data were collected via survey and analyzed using chi-square tests and logistic regression to evaluate adoption incentives and their effects on livelihoods. The findings demonstrate that agricultural technology adoption significantly increases household income and food security, thereby contributing to poverty alleviation (Marenya & Barrett, 2009; Mendola, 2003). Adoption rates are strongly influenced by factors such as education level, access to credit, extension services, and market proximity (Feder et al., 1985; Matuschke & Qaim, 2009). Persistent gender disparities continue to hinder universal participation in technological advancement (Zhou et al., 2018). These results underscore the necessity for institutional support, inclusive policies, and targeted interventions.

title: Preserving and Disseminating Ideas: The Information Carrier Trap and the Rise of the Industrial Revolution
affiliations: Tsinghua University - Institute of Economics and Central University of Finance and Economics (CUFE) - School of International Trade and Economics

detail.title: Preserving and Disseminating Ideas: The Information Carrier Trap and the Rise of the Industrial Revolution
detail.abstract: We develop an endogenous growth model with innovation in both information-carrier and production technologies. Information carriers preserve and disseminate knowledge, making nonrival knowledge an effective input for production technology innovation. Along the asymptotic balanced growth path, production technology and per capita consumption grow faster than information carrier technology. A calibrated transition path shows that R&D labor is initially concentrated in information carrier technology and later shifts toward production technology, generating an economic takeoff consistent with the timing of the British Industrial Revolution. In decentralized equilibrium, R&D labor underallocation is particularly pronounced in information carrier R&D, implying a higher wage subsidy rate than for production technology R&D. The model offers a new explanation for preindustrial stagnation---the information carrier trap---and hence for the transition to sustained growth.

title: The Effect of Local Content Requirements on Imports: Evidence from Canada's Renewable Energy Sector

detail.title: The Effect of Local Content Requirements on Imports: Evidence from Canada's Renewable Energy Sector

keywords: feed-in tariffs JEL Classification Numbers: F14

detail.abstract: I investigate whether local content requirements (LCRs), imposed by the Green Energy and Green Economy Act (GEGEA) of 2009 as an eligibility condition for generous feed-in tariffs to renewable energy producers, discourage renewable-energy-generation equipment imports in Ontario, Canada. While Canadian provinces have similar domestic importing conditions and overlapping renewable energy procurement policies, Ontario uniquely attached the LCR to a price-based procurement policy, allowing for comparable pre-trends in equipment imports between Ontario and other provinces. Empirical analyses using provincial import statistics find evidence of a reduction in importing products non-exclusive to renewable energy generation. Such reduced imports due to Ontario's LCRs in the wind energy sector incurred a deadweight loss that increased the implicit operation costs of the feed-in tariff program by 1.12 percent. However, there is little evidence that LCRs decreased equipment imports exclusive to renewable energy generation, suggesting that the policy effectiveness of LCRs is questionable.

title: 《Socialist Political Crisis: Bureaucratic Expansion and Ideological Devaluation》 (Concise Version) --A Historical Study of Socialist States Bureaucratic Expansion, Market Tension, and the Cyclicality of Ideological Devaluation: A Triple Dynamics of Socialist Political Crises from the Perspective of Matter-Cognition Historical Dynamics

detail.title: 《Socialist Political Crisis: Bureaucratic Expansion and Ideological Devaluation》 (Concise Version) --A Historical Study of Socialist States Bureaucratic Expansion, Market Tension, and the Cyclicality of Ideological Devaluation: A Triple Dynamics of Socialist Political Crises from the Perspective of Matter-Cognition Historical Dynamics
detail.abstract: This paper systematically constructs a threefold analytical framework for understanding political crises in socialist states, proceeding from the dynamic theory of matter-cognition historical dynamics. The first dynamic focuses on the internal positive-feedback coupling between bureaucratic expansion and ideological devaluation, showing how bureaucratic privilege shifts from functional management to self-serving interests, while ideological credibility is steadily consumed. The second dynamic introduces external variables-productivity difficulties, performance tensions relative to Western markets, and the influx of liberalizing thought-as factors accelerating the internal positive-feedback loop. The third dynamic elevates the analysis to the level of a cyclical law, arguing that socialist political crises, like capitalist economic crises, possess ineliminable structural roots in the eternal tension between the givenness of matter and the transcendence of cognition, but can be dynamically rebalanced through continuous institutional reform and the fulfillment of commitments. The collapse of the Soviet Union and self-correction in China serve as contrasting cases, revealing both the inevitability and the governability of this cyclical law.

detail.abstract: This paper questions the semi-strong efficiency in cryptomarkets by investigating daily return dynamics of four major coins. We build a flexible framework combining a Gaussian Mixture Model for regime identification, with penalised regression for state-conditional price dynamics. Our multidimensional approach identifies the respective contributions of price determinants. Sentiment variables play a major role in regime identification, alongside trading activity and recent price evolution. Conversely, state-conditional returns are primarily driven by macro-financial variables and recent price paths. This suggests that observed market erraticity reflects learning in price formation. Tail movements remain difficult to predict in density forecast, as next-day state remains difficult to predict. Although mean return predictability is weak at the daily horizon, directional predictability is non-negligible, especially during crash state when market stress intensifies. As such, these episodes reveal pockets of informational inefficiency, inconsistent with fully efficient markets. While belief formation follows common patterns across assets, heterogeneity arises from how these beliefs are aggregated into market expectations. Overshooting is the dominant mechanism. Seemingly, the system gravitates towards the calm state. However, the calm state forms an intermediate transitional phase as investors wait-and-see. Fear, uncertainty, and doubt operates in crash states. Behavioural mechanisms underpinning bull and bear markets remain ambiguous.

title: Sukavichinomics: Agricultural Innovation and Development

detail.title: Sukavichinomics: Agricultural Innovation and Development

detail.abstract: This study examines the application of the philosophy of Sukavichinomics in the development of Thailand's Agricultural sector, with a focus on the continuation and operationalization led by Dr. Nattapol Rangsitpol. The philosophy emphasizes human-centered development through the integration of Technology, Innovation, and sustainable economic mechanisms to enhance national competitiveness while addressing structural inequality, rural poverty, and long-term sustainability challenges. The research adopts a qualitative and descriptive approach based on literature review, policy analysis, and secondary data from relevant national development programs. The findings indicate that Sukavichinomics has been transformed from a conceptual framework into practical policy instruments and institutional mechanisms. In the agricultural sector, this transformation is reflected in the shift from subsistence-based farming toward a high-value Agro-Industrial systemdriven by knowledge and innovation. The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI), the Internet of Things (IoT), and Precision Agriculture has contributed to increased productivity, reduced production risk, improved resource efficiency, and enhanced income stability for farmers. Furthermore, initiatives such as MIND STAR, DIPROM GENIUS AGRO 360, and One Province One Agro-Industrial Community (OPOAI-C) demonstrate the development of a structured value-added agricultural ecosystem that strengthens human capital and links agriculture with industry. The study also finds strong alignment between Sukavichinomics and the Bio-Circular-Green (BCG) Economy Model, particularly in promoting sustainable resource utilization, environmental protection, and equitable economic growth. Overall, the findings suggest that Sukavichinomics provides a scalable development framework that integrates economic growth, social inclusion, and environmental sustainability, contributing to long-term national development and global applicability.

title: HPC-LLM-Bench: A Domain-Specific Language Model and Cross-Cluster Evaluation Framework for Research Computing Support and Education A Preprint

detail.title: HPC-LLM-Bench: A Domain-Specific Language Model and Cross-Cluster Evaluation Framework for Research Computing Support and Education A Preprint
detail.abstract: High-performance computing (HPC) environments are increasingly essential in modern education and scientific research, yet they remain difficult to use for many students and researchers. Large Language Models (LLMs) offer a promising solution by enabling natural language interaction with complex systems. However, existing evaluation approaches rely primarily on general-purpose metrics that fail to capture domain-specific usefulness. This paper presents HPC-LLM-Bench, a unified framework that combines a domain-specific language model (HPC-LLM) with a novel evaluation methodology tailored for research computing. In addition to traditional metrics such as semantic similarity and latency, we introduce new evaluation dimensions including actionability, command correctness, hallucination risk, instruction coverage, and educational value. We evaluate HPC-LLM against several general-purpose models across two HPC environments (CAMSA and Jetstream) using a dataset of HPC-related prompts. Results show that while general models perform well on traditional NLP metrics, HPC-LLM achieves better performance in domain-specific usability and task-oriented responses. Furthermore, we observe system-level performance variability across clusters, highlighting the importance of evaluating LLMs under realistic deployment conditions.

title: Learning from the Book: AI Evidence on Short-Run Market Efficiency
affiliations: Macquarie University - Faculty of Business and Economics and Macquarie Graduate School of Management

detail.title: Learning from the Book: AI Evidence on Short-Run Market Efficiency
detail.abstract: This paper examines short-run weak-form efficiency and price discovery on a major electronic limit-order-book market using proprietary high-frequency NSE data. We combine structural microstructure tools with modern AIbased supervised learning-primarily Random Forests-to capture non-linear orderbook patterns, classify algorithmic versus non-algorithmic traders, and relate their behaviour to the efficient price. Using full-depth orderbook features and new dispersion-based metrics, we find that proprietary algorithmic traders (HFTs) contribute nearly half of price discovery, while other groups contribute little to the permanent component of prices. Orderbook imbalance and slope contain the most predictive information, and higher algorithmic activity, tighter spreads, and heavier trading reduce short-horizon price predictability, consistent with improved efficiency. Overall, algorithmic activity both decreases predictability and enhances information incorporation, illustrating how AI can serve as both a predictive tool and an economic lens for understanding the role of automated trading in shaping short-run market quality.

title: Believe, But Verify? The Psychology of Poverty and Social Identity Economics in African Economies: Does Co-Ethnicity with the President Fuel Favoritism, and Which Political Settlements Can Distribute National Cake Benefits?

detail.title: Believe, But Verify? The Psychology of Poverty and Social Identity Economics in African Economies: Does Co-Ethnicity with the President Fuel Favoritism, and Which Political Settlements Can Distribute National Cake Benefits?

keywords: Behavioral Economics and Political economy i

detail.abstract: This study examines the interaction between the psychology of poverty, social identity economics, and political settlements in explaining whether co-ethnicity with the president fuels political favoritism in Africa, and how institutions can address it. It is based on a systematic review of 113 studies using the PRISMA protocol, drawing from development economics, behavioral economics, social identity theory, and political economy literature. Findings show that co-ethnic favoritism exists but is not universal. Poverty and scarcity reduce cognitive capacity , Social identity strongly shapes government resource allocation, with evidence of higher spending toward co-ethnic groups. Coethnicity with the president can fuel favoritism, though effects vary across countries. Inclusive political settlements reduce favoritism, while exclusive systems reinforce it. The study concludes that addressing this issue requires coordinated reforms. Inclusive, rule-based systems with power-sharing, accountability, and strong institutions are most effective in reducing favoritism and promoting fair governance. The study recommends that despite co-ethnicity with the president does fueling favoritism, although it is neither universal nor uniform, co-ethnicity with the president itself is not a problem, since it does not have heart or knowledge; rather, policymakers should reduce the rate of stereotypes (in-group "we" and out-group "they") to zero, put long-term public interest above short-term political survival, and boost path dependency.

title: The Cryptoeconomy as a Concentrated Growth Culture
affiliations: Royal Melbourne Institute of Technology (RMIT University) and Royal Melbourne Institute of Technology (RMIT University)

detail.title: The Cryptoeconomy as a Concentrated Growth Culture
detail.abstract: This chapter argues that crypto is not merely a technological or financial innovation, but the most concentrated culture of institutional improvement since the Enlightenment. Drawing on Nobel Laureate Joel Mokyr's body of work, we frame the cryptoeconomy as a community that legitimises experimentation, rewards useful knowledge, and sustains belief in progress. Rather than treating growth as the product of incentives or formal institutions alone, Mokyr emphasised the cultural norms and intellectual networks that protect novelty and enable cumulative improvement. The cryptoeconomy's open knowledge communities, composable institutional toolkits, and embedded incentive structures are a public global laboratory for institutional evolution. This chapter argues that Mokyr's cultural framework is a useful lens for understanding crypto as a sustained experiment in building new institutions rather than reforming old ones.

title: The Genesis of "Alpha": An Artefact of Methodological Ambiguity

detail.title: The Genesis of "Alpha": An Artefact of Methodological Ambiguity
detail.abstract: Classical performance measurement in modern asset-pricing theory is anchored in benchmark-adjusted excess return—commonly termed alpha (α)—and in a family of reward-to-risk ratios built upon it. Once default risk is explicitly incorporated into the standard asset-pricing framework (Sharpe, 1964; Lintner, 1965; Mossin, 1966) and its extensions (Merton, 1973; Fama and French, 1993; Carhart, 1997; Fama and French, 2015; Idzorek and Ibbotson, 2021), however, a systematic bias in the classical metrics becomes apparent. This concern applies to Jensen's alpha (Jensen, 1968), the Sharpe ratio (Sharpe, 1966), the Treynor ratio (Treynor, 1965), the Sortino ratio (Sortino and van der Meer, 1991), the Information ratio (Treynor and Black, 1973; Grinold, 1989), and the Modigliani measure (Modigliani and Modigliani, 1997), the Graham–Harvey measure (Graham and Harvey, 1996), as well as to alternative performance measures derived from the payoff-distribution model (Dybvig, 1988). Contrary to its conventional interpretation, positive excess performance need not indicate superior skill: it may instead reflect higher unmodelled default exposure, insufficient diversification, or an inefficient dynamic investment strategy, combined with favorable no-default realizations, implying that the appearance of alpha may itself be a methodological artefact.

detail.abstract: Enterprise AI systems are moving from advisory use toward bounded operational autonomy. That shift creates a control problem: organizations must decide how probabilistic models can be permitted to trigger deterministic actions in environments constrained by security, compliance, privacy, and operational reliability. This paper frames that mismatch as the Probabilistic Execution Gap. To address it, we propose a governance-first reference architecture built around two coupled ideas: a five-zone trustboundary model that separates agent planning from execution, and a multi-agent quorum model that treats every autonomous proposal as draft output until it is validated by deterministic policy controls and, where required, qualified human oversight. The paper contributes a Governance Chokepoint between planning and action, a human-in-the-loop center of excellence, a privacy proxy for masked review, an operational incident model, and a meta-governance lifecycle for changes to the governance layer itself. The result is an implementation-oriented framework for bounded enterprise agency. The framework is conceptual rather than experimentally validated; empirical deployment studies remain future work.

title: The Blind Spot of the Twin Transition: Regulating the Environmental Footprint Of Large Language Models in the UK and EU

detail.title: The Blind Spot of the Twin Transition: Regulating the Environmental Footprint Of Large Language Models in the UK and EU
detail.abstract: The European Union and the United Kingdom are simultaneously pursuing a Twin Transition towards digital transformation and climate neutrality, predicated on the assumption that these goals are synergistic. However, the exponential rise of Large Language Models (LLMs) exposes a critical tension in this narrative: the massive energy, water, and carbon demands of compute threaten to undermine net-zero targets. This article provides a comparative doctrinal analysis of the emerging regulatory landscapes, specifically juxtaposing the EU's AI Act and Ecodesign frameworks against the UK's proinnovation White Paper approach and Environment Act 2021. It argues that a regulatory blind spot persists in both jurisdictions. Traditional environmental law remains fixated on physical industrial pollution, while nascent digital regulation prioritizes safety, bias, and privacy over sustainability. Consequently, the material environmental footprint of generative AI remains largely externalized. The article concludes that current procedural transparency mandates are insufficient to mitigate this growing impact. To resolve the Twin Transition paradox, legal frameworks must evolve to substantively integrate compute intensity into Environmental Impact Assessments and public procurement standards, treating digital infrastructure as a critical resource challenge rather than a purely virtual service.

title: A Dynamic Evaluative Model of Motivation: Symbolic-Functional Reweighting and Constraint-Based Selection

detail.title: A Dynamic Evaluative Model of Motivation: Symbolic-Functional Reweighting and Constraint-Based Selection

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no known conflicts of interest or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.

detail.abstract:
This article develops a quasi-formal dynamic model of motivation that departs from hierarchical and stage-based accounts. Instead of representing motivation as progression through ordered needs, the proposed framework conceptualizes it as a process of continuous evaluation within a field of competing objects.

At the core of the model is a unified evaluative structure in which each object is assessed in terms of four co-present components: symbolic value, functional return, symbolic constraints, and functional constraints. Behavioral selection emerges from comparative evaluation across alternatives, rather than from transitions between predefined levels.

Motivational dynamics are governed by context-sensitive reweighting and threshold-dependent transitions. Changes in behavior do not follow directly from variations in inputs, but occur when differences in net motivational value exceed a context-dependent sensitivity boundary, producing nonlinear and discontinuous patterns of change. Within this structure, motivational change is driven by shifts in weighting parameters and constraint dynamics.

The framework generates empirically testable predictions, including threshold-driven behavioral transitions, sensitivity to symbolic amplification, and systematic modulation of choice under varying symbolic and functional constraint conditions. By formalizing symbolic–functional interaction within a unified evaluative architecture, the model provides a structurally grounded alternative to hierarchical theories of motivation.

This approach establishes a foundation for empirical investigation, computational modeling, and cross-domain applications in decision-making, collective behavior, and cognitive-neural systems.

title: Per-Market Information Leakage and Order-Flow Skill: Two Methodological Lenses on Informed Trading in Decentralized Prediction Markets

detail.title: Per-Market Information Leakage and Order-Flow Skill: Two Methodological Lenses on Informed Trading in Decentralized Prediction Markets
detail.abstract:
April 2026 saw notable methodological convergence in the academic
study of informed trading on decentralized prediction markets.
Three methodological approaches surfaced almost simultaneously,
each addressing the same body of documented cases on Polymarket but
operating at different methodological layers: Mitts and Ofir (2026)
apply a composite statistical screen to over 210,000 wallet–market
pairs and estimate $143 million in aggregate anomalous profit;
Gomez-Cram, Guo, Jensen, and Kung (2026) apply an event-level
sign-randomization test to the platform's complete transaction
history, classifying 3.14% of accounts as "skilled winners" who
drive most price discovery, and separately apply a single-event
lifecycle-and-conviction heuristic that flags 1,950 accounts as
"insiders"; Nechepurenko (2026) develops the Information Leakage
Score (ILS) framework, which quantifies per-market information
front-loading at the article-derived public-event timestamp.

This paper provides a methodological comparison and a sketch of how
the approaches combine. The central organizing claim is that these
are three distinct layers of detection, not three competing methods
on a single layer. Sign-randomization, in particular, is best
understood as an account-level test of persistent directional skill
conditional on opportunity selection — not a direct test of insider
trading, and not a per-market measure. The heuristic insider flag
in Gomez-Cram et al. (2026) is methodologically separate from their
skill classifier, applies to a population (single-event,
recently-created accounts) that the skill classifier explicitly
excludes by design, and has unknown precision against an external
labelled set. The Polymarket sample on which all three approaches
are evaluated pools politics, sports, crypto, and other categories
with structurally different information technologies, so a
platform-wide "skilled winner" classification is mechanism-ambiguous,
and category-conditioned decompositions are required before the
methodology can be used as a surveillance layer.

The January 2026 U.S.–Venezuela operation cluster, where the U.S.
Department of Justice indictment of Master Sergeant Gannon Van Dyke
provides a rare external enforcement benchmark on at least one
alleged informed trader, illustrates how the layers stack:
account-level lifecycle heuristics identify a small set of
suspicious accounts with face-valid enforcement alignment; legal
investigation addresses whether a specific trader actually possessed
non-public information; per-market scoring would quantify how much
information was leaked into each contract before public observation.
None of the three layers subsumes the others, and a combined
surveillance pipeline gains in precision precisely because each
layer filters a different dimension of the problem.

title: Empirical Evaluation of Deadline-Resolved Information Leakage on Documented Polymarket Insider Cases

detail.title: Empirical Evaluation of Deadline-Resolved Information Leakage on Documented Polymarket Insider Cases

keywords: empirical evaluation JEL Classication: D82 (Asymmetric and Private Information)

detail.abstract:
This paper reports an end-to-end empirical evaluation of the
deadline-Information Leakage Score (ILS-dl) extension introduced in
the companion methodology paper. The deadline-ILS extends the
original ILS to deadline-resolved prediction-market contracts — the
dominant structural form of publicly documented insider trading on
Polymarket. We anchor the evaluation in the 2026 U.S.–Iran conflict
cluster of the ForesightFlow Insider Cases (FFIC) inventory, the
largest documented deadline cluster in the public-reporting record.
The evaluation has four parts: per-category exponential-hazard rate
estimation for the time-to-event distribution; a single-case ILS-dl
computation on the cleanest applicable FFIC market; cross-market
wallet analysis across two cluster contracts; and the methodological
refinements that the evaluation surfaces.

The hazard-rate estimation produces an adequate exponential fit for
military/geopolitics markets (KS p = 0.609, half-life 2.3 days) and
a preliminary fit for corporate-disclosure markets (n = 5). The
regulatory-decision category is rejected as bimodal (p = 0.013) and
requires sub-categorization. On the largest applicable FFIC contract
("US forces enter Iran by April 30," $269M cumulative volume), the
article-derived public-event timestamp yields ILS-dl = +0.113 versus
a resolution-anchored proxy value of −0.331: a 0.444 shift in
magnitude on opposite sides of zero, demonstrating that the
extension distinguishes signal from proxy artefact. The pre-event
drift is mild rather than concentrated, and short-window variants
(30-min, 2-hour) are exactly zero, ruling out a last-minute informed
spike. Cross-market wallet analysis identifies 332 wallets active
in both major Iran-cluster markets, but the available trade history
covers only the resolution-settlement window; the cross-market
signal is therefore settlement arbitrage rather than pre-event
coordination, and converting this diagnostic into a coordination-
signal diagnostic requires continuous per-trade collection from
market opening.

We treat the present evaluation as a methodological proof of concept
supported by a single illustrative case, not a population-level
evaluation. Five concrete refinements bound any future scaling:
positive-τ requirement, regulatory sub-categorization,
corporate-disclosure sample expansion, continuous CLOB price
collection, and continuous per-trade collection from market opening.
Both data resources used here — the FFIC inventory and the
resolution-typology classification of the 911,237-market Polymarket
corpus — are released as separate datasets at github.com/ForesightFlow/datasets.

title: ForesightFlow: An Information Leakage Score Framework for Prediction Markets

detail.title: ForesightFlow: An Information Leakage Score Framework for Prediction Markets
detail.abstract:
ForesightFlow is an Information Leakage Score (ILS) framework for
detecting informed trading on decentralized prediction markets. For
an event-resolved binary market, the score quantifies the fraction
of the terminal information move priced in before the public news
event. Three operational scope conditions — edge effect, non-trivial
total move, and anchor sensitivity — are stated as preconditions for
interpretation. The score admits a Murphy-decomposition reading that
connects label generation to the proper-scoring-rule literature.

A pilot empirical evaluation surfaces three findings. First, a
resolution-anchored proxy for the public-event timestamp does not
separate event-resolved markets from a matched control population
(Mann–Whitney p = 1×10⁻⁶, separation reversed), demonstrating that
proxy quality is itself a binding constraint on the framework.
Second, the article-derived timestamp on a single high-stakes case
shifts the score by 0.444 in magnitude relative to the proxy and
lies on the opposite side of zero, indicating that anchor recovery
materially changes the substantive reading. Third, an audit of the
publicly documented Polymarket insider record reveals that documented
cases are systematically deadline-resolved, falling outside the
original ILS scope (0 of 24 FFIC inventory markets satisfied
original scope conditions).

This last finding motivates a deadline-ILS extension introduced in
Section 7, anchored at the public-event timestamp rather than the
news timestamp, and equipped with a per-category exponential hazard
baseline for the time-to-event distribution. The extension closes
the gap between the methodology and the population in which insider
trading has been empirically documented. An end-to-end empirical
evaluation of the extension on the 2026 U.S.–Iran conflict cluster
is reported in a companion paper. We release the ForesightFlow
Insider Cases (FFIC) inventory, the resolution-typology
classification of the 911,237-market Polymarket corpus, and all
system code openly at github.com/ForesightFlow.

title: Domestic work in EU law: the relevance of EU employment law in challenging domestic workers' vulnerability

detail.title: Domestic work in EU law: the relevance of EU employment law in challenging domestic workers' vulnerability
detail.abstract: The importance of EU employment law sources as tools to challenge the vulnerability of domestic workers has surprisingly been a neglected theme in the growing legal scholarship on paid domestic work in Europe. This is due to a flawed assumption that EU employment law does not apply to domestic workers. I challenge this assumption and provide a more nuanced picture. My aim is twofold: to show clearly when EU employment law applies to domestic workers and what rights and protections they can derive. From this follows the broader conclusion that EU employment law is an important but misunderstood resource for domestic workers.

title: Institutionalization of International Labor Rights had Less Impact in Undivided India Due to Colonial Legacy and Social Prejudice to Manual Labor

detail.title: Institutionalization of International Labor Rights had Less Impact in Undivided India Due to Colonial Legacy and Social Prejudice to Manual Labor
detail.abstract:
This article explores the growth and significance of international labour rights in pre-partitioned India in the context of colonial policies and caste-based social divisions, and their role in shaping labour rights. While the creation of the International Labour Organization (ILO) in 1919 marked a world commitment to decent and humane working conditions, this was not translated to colonial India due to British economic interests and oppressive labour legislation. The paper examines how significant laws like the Factories Act, 1881 and the Indian Trade Union Act, 1926 were largely enshrinements of colonial policy and not in the service of workers. It also examines the impact of caste discrimination on labour solidarity and its impact on collective bargaining.

Nonetheless, the paper outlines how labour movements slowly began to form, with the help of nationalist leaders and trade unions, and accompanied early labour reforms to increase awareness. It also examines the big bang effects of colonial labour laws on post-independence labour laws, such as the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. The research concludes that although the positive impact of international labour rights was limited in the colonial era, they indirectly contributed to the framework of labour rights in South Asia.

title: Sample Origin Sensitivity in GSADF Bubble Detection

detail.title: Sample Origin Sensitivity in GSADF Bubble Detection

declarations.funderStatement: Generously funded by my Father Ahmed Madkhali

detail.abstract:
The Generalised Supremum Augmented Dickey Fuller (GSADF) test of PSY (2015) is the dominant method for detecting and date-stamping speculative bubbles. The test’s feasibility constraint r2 - r1 ≥ r0 implies a sample-design requirement not previously operationalised: a bubble originating at τe can contribute to the GSADF supremum only if the sample begins at or before τe - r0T. This dissertation formulates this requirement as a checkable inequality—the Baseline Coverage Condition (BCC)—derived directly from PSY’s feasibility constraint, and documents its empirical bite. Two mechanical properties govern its signature: the GSADF statistic degrades monotonically under progressive trimming, and a discrete drop when the dominant bubble window exits the feasible set. A Monte Carlo experiment across a (T, σ) grid establishes that under a baseline explosive DGP, T ≥ 600–800 daily observations are required for empirical size to converge to nominal levels; uncorrected 50% rejection is achieved at T ≈ 400 but at a 23% null distortion against a 5% nominal level, so smaller-sample power figures should be read as upper bounds.


The BCC is validated through (i) one-to-one replication of Cheung et al. (2015), (ii) progressive trimming on three published Bitcoin studies showing the predicted drop within 1–4 months of the BCC threshold, and (iii) application to Ethereum across six series: four exchanges (Coinbase, Kraken, Binance, OKX) and two VWAP composites (Kraken+Coinbase, Global ETH via CryptoCompare CCCAGG). The four long-history BCC-satisfying series reject at 95%; Binance and OKX, BCC-violating for the 2017 ICO episode, fail. Alignment converges all GSADF statistics into a 0.015-wide band; controlled experiments separate the alignment confound, with a pure start-shift past the BCC threshold reproducing the failure (GSADF: 4.529 ↔ 2.461, matching aligned Coinbase to three decimals) and a length-matched control with start preserved leaving the rejection intact (GSADF= 4.533). Cross-exchange concordance is high where samples overlap, and the VWAP composites produce nested chronologies. The contribution is a specification diagnostic that complements the PSY framework, not a critique of it.

title:
THE FUTURE OF WORK: AI’S DISRUPTION IN MARKETING
PROFESSIONALS

detail.title:
THE FUTURE OF WORK: AI’S DISRUPTION IN MARKETING
PROFESSIONALS
detail.abstract:
Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming the global workforce,
particularly in knowledge-intensive domains such as marketing.
Traditionally, marketing relied on human creativity, intuition, and
experience; however, the integration of AI has shifted the focus toward
data-driven decision-making, automation, and predictive analytics. AI
technologies enable marketers to process vast datasets, personalize
customer interactions, and optimize campaigns in real time.
This research paper examines how AI is disrupting marketing
professionals by transforming job roles, skill requirements, and
organizational structures. While AI enhances efficiency and
productivity, it also raises concerns regarding job displacement, skill
gaps, and ethical challenges. The study highlights that AI does not
replace marketers entirely but augments their capabilities, requiring
professionals to adapt to new technologies and develop hybrid skills.

title: ForesightFlow: Real-Time Detection of Informed Trading in Decentralized Prediction Markets

detail.title: ForesightFlow: Real-Time Detection of Informed Trading in Decentralized Prediction Markets
detail.abstract:
Decentralized prediction markets such as Polymarket aggregate
dispersed beliefs into continuously updated price signals, but their
on-chain transparency and pseudonymous participation also make them
an unusually fertile environment for informed trading on material
non-public information. Recent empirical work has documented hundreds
of millions of dollars in anomalous profits on Polymarket between
2024 and 2026; existing detection approaches are almost exclusively
post-hoc and offer no actionable signal during the window when
informed flow is actually moving prices.

We propose ForesightFlow, a real-time detection framework that
combines classical microstructure measures of informed trading —
adapted to the discrete, bounded structure of binary outcome
markets — with on-chain wallet features unique to decentralized
platforms. We introduce the Information Leakage Score (ILS), a label
generator that quantifies how much of a market's terminal information
move was priced in before the corresponding public news event, and
show that ILS admits a clean interpretation in terms of the Murphy
decomposition of the Brier score. As an empirical anchor we release
the ForesightFlow Insider Cases (FFIC) inventory, a curated
validation set mapping eight publicly documented insider episodes to
concrete Polymarket market identifiers. The historical-backfill stage
of the data pipeline is operational, indexing 911,237 markets
(865,725 resolved) and 17.9 million trades across 10,410 markets
above the $50K volume cutoff at which subgraph trade history becomes
reliably available.

A pilot empirical study tightens the methodology in three ways: a
resolution-anchored proxy for T_news does not separate event-resolved
markets from a matched control population; high ILS on high-consensus
markets reflects a formula edge effect; and the proxy-based ILS
distribution is not robust to anchor choice. We specify three
operational scope conditions for ILS — restriction to event-resolved
markets with substantive uncertainty at T_open, recovery of
article-derived T_news, and a robustness check across multiple anchor
offsets. A proof-of-concept article-derived T_news recovery on the
Epstein-files Barak market shifts ILS only from 0.553 to 0.570
relative to the proxy, suggesting that proxy quality was not the
binding constraint and that wallet-level features rather than ILS
alone are required to identify informed flow.

An attempt to scale to the full FFIC inventory revealed that
documented insider cases are systematically deadline-resolved ("Will
event X occur by date Y?"), falling outside the original ILS scope.
We extend the score to a deadline-ILS variant anchored to the
underlying event timestamp, implement a categorical exponential-hazard
baseline for the time-to-event distribution, and apply the extension
to the 2026 U.S.–Iran conflict cluster. On the cleanest applicable
case ("US forces enter Iran by April 30," $269M cumulative volume),
the deadline-ILS shifts from −0.331 at the resolution-anchored proxy
to +0.113 at the article-derived event timestamp, demonstrating that
the extension distinguishes signal from proxy artefact. The empirical
evaluation surfaces five concrete methodological refinements that
constrain any future application of the framework: a positive lead-
time requirement, regulatory sub-categorization, corporate-disclosure
sample expansion, continuous CLOB price collection, and continuous
per-trade collection from market opening.

System code, the FFIC inventory, and a full resolution-typology
classification of the 911,237-market corpus are released openly at
github.com/ForesightFlow.

title: Scaling in a Complex Ecosystem Africa, Structure, and the Mathematics of Opportunity

detail.title: Scaling in a Complex Ecosystem Africa, Structure, and the Mathematics of Opportunity
detail.abstract: The persistent difficulty of scaling development interventions in Africa is often framed as a failure of finance, policy, or implementation. This paper argues that such framings are superficial. The deeper issue lies in a misreading of Africa as a system. Africa is not a collection of projects, but a complex, evolving ecosystem shaped by the interaction of state, market, and society. Within this system, scaling is not replication but emergence. Drawing on complexity science, institutional economics, and African policy discourse, this paper develops a structural account of why scaling fails and where opportunities lie. It introduces holonomic moments as windows for transformation, examines domestic money pools as control structures, and reframes infrastructure as an operator acting on system states. The conclusion is direct: scale in Africa must be cultivated through systemic understanding, institutional alignment, and deliberate engagement with crisis.

title: THE EUROPEAN UNION ENGAGEMENT ON CLIMATE ACTIONS WITH COUNTRIES FROM ASIA-PACIFIC REGION CASE STUDY: ESTABLISHING THE JUST ENERGY TRANSITION PARTNERSHIP WITH VIET NAM

detail.abstract: In order to achieve the climate goals of the Paris Agreement and manage the transition to sustainable, climate-resilient and climate-neutral development, rapid and deep greenhouse gas reductions were necessary. Consequently, at the 26th UN Climate Change Conference in Glasgow (COP26) it was announced the first "Just Energy Transition Partnership" (JETP) as a new plurilateral structure for accelerating the phase-out of fossil fuels. Taking into account that the fight against climate change has reached a critical turning point in 2025 - a year marked by geopolitical tensions and economic risks - the main purpose of this study is to highlight the instruments and tools used by EU to deepen climate cooperation with other countries, especially within existing JETPs with countries from Asia Pacific region. In this context, considering the Viet Nam’s commitments announced at the 26th UN Climate Change Conference in Glasgow (COP26), including a net-zero emissions target by 2050, a subsequent aim of this study is to deepen and clarify the aspects related to the adoption and implementation of the Just Energy Transition Partnership (JETP) with Viet Nam.

title: Exploring the Impact of Monitoring and Evaluation Systems on Early Childhood Care and Education in India: A case study of Anganwadi Workers in Maharashtra

detail.title: Exploring the Impact of Monitoring and Evaluation Systems on Early Childhood Care and Education in India: A case study of Anganwadi Workers in Maharashtra
detail.abstract: Anganwadi Workers (AWWs) are central to delivering Early Childhood Care and Education (ECCE) services in India, yet their work is increasingly shaped by Monitoring and Evaluation (M&E) systems. This study examines how these systems affect AWWs’ roles and service delivery. Based on qualitative interviews with AWWs and Supervisors in Maharashtra, conducted during ongoing worker protests, the study highlights the everyday realities of frontline implementation. Findings show that ECCE delivery is dominated by administrative and data-related tasks, reinforced by weak infrastructure, ambiguous goals, and metric-based accountability. This creates a disconnect between AWWs’ perceived roles as educators and their routine clerical responsibilities. In response, workers adopt coping strategies such as overtime work and informal data practices. The study argues that M&E systems function primarily as tools of state performance rather than program improvement, and calls for greater frontline discretion and context-sensitive design to enhance ECCE outcomes.

title: Directional Land Optimisation for Improving Crop Yield and Water Efficiency: A Field-Based Study in Sugarcane Farming

detail.title: Directional Land Optimisation for Improving Crop Yield and Water Efficiency: A Field-Based Study in Sugarcane Farming
detail.abstract: Sugarcane is a water-intensive crop highly vulnerable to drought stress and inefficient land management. This study evaluates the impact of directional land optimisation and spatial field layout on crop yield, soil moisture, and irrigation efficiency. A comparative field experiment was conducted across control and intervention farms, where the intervention involved structured alignment of crop rows, water placement, and open zones based on directional principles. Results indicate that an optimised spatial configuration can improve yield (≈approximately 15-20%), reduce water usage (≈approximately 20-25%), and enhance soil moisture retention. The findings suggest that traditional land-orientation knowledge, when interpreted scientifically, may offer a low-cost complementary approach to sustainable agriculture.

title: The Schooling Lag Rank Persistence and the Measurement of Intergenerational Educational Mobility

detail.title: The Schooling Lag Rank Persistence and the Measurement of Intergenerational Educational Mobility
detail.abstract: The intergenerational elasticity (IGE) of education conflates two distinct phenomena: changes in positional persistence and the mechanical compression of schooling distributions across generations. The rank-rank regression, designed for continuous income, cannot resolve this conflation because discrete education generates massive ties that corrupt the estimand. I propose the schooling lag-a respondent's deviation from their census-based cohort-sex mean schooling, subsequently ranked-which resolves both problems simultaneously. A four-object decomposition nests the IGE, the demeaned-level slope, the rank-of-levels slope, and the rank-of-lags slope within a unified variance hierarchy, showing how each transformation removes a distinct source of bias, and that the Chetty-style rank-of-levels does not resolve the tie problem. Applied to eighteen waves of Latinobarómetro (1998-2023) across eighteen Latin American countries, the gap between the IGE and the within-cohort correlation ρ lag is widening over time (p < 0.001), implying that an increasing share of the measured IGE decline is distributional artifact. The population-weighted artifact share is approximately 70% (bootstrap 95% CI: [42%, 98%]), ranging from 41% to 76% across weighting schemes. Absolute upward mobility-the probability that a child exceeds their parent's education-is rising at 0.38 percentage points per year (p < 0.001), but rank-based upward mobility is flat (p = 0.71): access expansion is working, but positional persistence is not weakening. The decomposition reshuffles country mobility rankings and 1 reveals that only one of eighteen countries-Colombia-shows statistically significant improvement in both the standard and corrected measures.

title: Book Review -Silent Spring by Rachel Carson

detail.title: Book Review -Silent Spring by Rachel Carson
detail.abstract: The major premise of the book was to exemplify how insecticides, in particular, the chlorinated hydrocarbons and organic phosphorus, can contribute to altering the cellular processes of plants and, in the case of organisms, changing the genetic structure. The author, Rachel Carson, had meticulously dealt with the impacts of insecticides on the biosphere through anecdotes and a strong theoretical backing from the bioscience discipline. Although the theoretical inference had helped us understand the extent of insecticide usage by analysing the nature of such chemical compounds, the whole discourse built can be perceived as an eye-opener for a layman who is not aware of such implications. Likewise, a journalistic stance can be felt while going through the short anecdotes, which are conjoined with the scientific backing.

detail.abstract:
This working paper examines how leveraged buyout analysis must be adapted when applied to emerging markets, using India as the central case. The conventional LBO model, developed primarily in the United States and Western Europe, assumes deep acquisition-finance markets, predictable debt enforcement, creditor coordination, and the ability to place meaningful leverage close to operating-company cash flows. These assumptions do not transfer cleanly to India.

The paper argues that Indian buyouts should not be understood as weaker versions of developed-market LBOs, but as adapted buyout structures shaped by legal, regulatory, credit-market, ownership, and exit-route constraints. It combines conceptual analysis with a coded public-source dataset of twenty India-linked buyout, control, and acquisition-finance transactions, a regulatory-friction scoring framework, and an illustrative standard-versus-India-adapted LBO model.

The findings suggest that India-adapted buyouts rely less on high acquisition leverage and more on growth, governance improvement, structured private credit, hybrid instruments, promoter negotiation, and exit planning. The paper contributes a practical methodological framework for researchers, private equity professionals, private credit investors, and finance students seeking to distinguish developed-market LBO mechanics from emerging-market buyout realities. The paper is intended as an evidence-backed working paper and does not constitute legal, tax, investment, or financial advice.

title: The Dignity Deficit: Why AI Policy Frameworks Miss the Point

detail.title: The Dignity Deficit: Why AI Policy Frameworks Miss the Point
detail.abstract:
Global AI policy operates almost entirely inside a labour economics frame. Governments count jobs at risk, design reskilling pipelines, debate universal basic income, and argue about which industries will recover and which will not. Even the most sophisticated critics of AI's economic impact, such as Daron Acemoglu's work on "the wrong kind of AI," are still arguing about the distribution of economic output. This paper argues that the frame itself is the problem.

The actual casualty of AI-scale disruption is not employment. It is 'significance': the social condition in which human judgment, effort, and presence are experienced as mattering, both by the individual and by the communities around them. Significance is not dignity in the narrow sense that AI ethics discourse has so far invoked, which tends to mean freedom from bias or protection from surveillance. Significance is structural, relational, and distributed. It is produced and destroyed not in isolated transactions but in the social architectures through which communities recognize human contribution.

This matters most acutely in the Global South, and particularly in India, where significance is not individuated in the Western therapeutic sense but is deeply embedded in caste, family, and community ecologies. When AI displaces a software engineer in Bengaluru or a paralegal in Mumbai, it does not merely take income. It takes the social legibility that the role carried: the position in the family hierarchy, the authority within the community, the answer to the question "what do you do?" that has organized self-worth for generations.

The paper argues that policy designed around job displacement will actively worsen the dignity deficit, because it treats people as economic units to be reabsorbed into the market rather than as relational beings embedded in systems of recognition. I propose instead a set of relational governance principles that treat the preservation of social architectures for human contribution as a policy goal in its own right.

title: PAAPM+: A Strategy-Adjusted AI Asset Pricing Model Integrating Governance Quality with Lifecycle Position to Quantify the Governance Decay Premium in Board-Level AI Investment

detail.abstract: Every year, UK boards commit billions of pounds to AI investment on the basis of a question they cannot answer: not what is this system returning today, but whether that return is building toward something sustainable or eroding toward a governance crisis that financial statements will only reveal when it is too late to prevent. This paper introduces PAAPM+ — the Picken AI Asset Pricing Model (Strategy-Adjusted) — as the first financially grounded framework to address the trajectory question at board level. PAAPM+ extends the established PAAPM governance-adjusted return model by incorporating a three-factor Lifecycle Multiplier, producing a strategy-adjusted expected return for each AI system in a board's portfolio. The central novel contribution is the Governance Decay Premium (GDP_AI): a formally defined financial metric that quantifies, in pounds per annum, the value being destroyed by governance trajectory deterioration before that destruction appears in financial statements. Applied to three AI systems in a synthetic NHS foundation trust, PAAPM+ identifies £187,400 in recoverable governance value and £41,157 in annual value destruction invisible to every governance framework currently in operation.

detail.abstract: This paper delves into the convergence of fashion and technology, commonly referred to as “fashtech,” through the analytical framework of Pierre Bourdieu’s concept of capital. As the fashion industry embraces technological advancements – from smart textiles and wearable devices to digital platforms and artificial intelligence – the traditional forms of capital outlined by Bourdieu (economic, cultural, social, and symbolic) undergo significant transformation and redefinition. By revisiting Bourdieu’s theories, the study examines how fashtech not only reshapes the distribution and accumulation of these capitals but also creates new avenues for their enhancement and expression. For instance, technological innovations enhance cultural capital by enabling innovative design and creative expression, while digital networking platforms expand social capital through enhanced connectivity and influencer ecosystems. Additionally, the integration of technology elevates symbolic capital by redefining brand prestige and consumer identity in a digitally-driven marketplace. Furthermore, the study considers the role of intellectual property (IP), highlighting how IP introduces complexities that are not entirely encompassed by Bourdieu’s traditional framework of capital. This analysis highlights the intricate ways in which fashtech influences and is influenced by the various forms of capital, offering a comprehensive understanding of power dynamics and status within the modern fashion landscape. Ultimately, the paper contributes to both fashion studies and sociological theory by demonstrating the enduring relevance of Bourdieu’s concepts in interpreting the ongoing evolution of the fashion industry in the digital age.

title: Gradient-Informed Hamiltonian Monte Carlo for Multicomponent CALPHAD Model Optimization and Uncertainty Quantification

detail.title: Gradient-Informed Hamiltonian Monte Carlo for Multicomponent CALPHAD Model Optimization and Uncertainty Quantification
detail.abstract: CALPHAD model parameter optimization is inherently challenging due to non-smooth objective functions, high-dimensional parameter spaces, and the need for uncertainty quantification (UQ). Traditional weighted nonlinear least squares approaches are computationally efficient but local, whereas black-box global optimizers and ensemble Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods provide broader exploration at substantial computational cost. The objective of this work is to combine the global exploration capability of gradient-informed Hamiltonian Monte Carlo--specifically the No-U-Turn Sampler (NUTS)--with local deterministic refinement using BFGS to efficiently optimize multicomponent CALPHAD models with minimal manual intervention. Analytic gradients are computed via the Jansson derivative framework. The methodology is demonstrated on the Cr-Fe binary system and extended to the Cr-Fe-Ni ternary system with 32 degrees of freedom. For Cr-Fe, NUTS achieves comparable or superior optimality relative to ensemble MCMC while requiring over an order-of-magnitude fewer likelihood evaluations. Parameter uncertainties are quantified through NUTS sampling and propagated to thermodynamic observables using local expansion, demonstrating a novel modular approach that combines binary and ternary parameter subsets without requiring global relaxation. These results establish gradient-informed exploration as a scalable strategy for multicomponent CALPHAD optimization and provide a practical route toward efficient higher-order database development with quantified uncertainty.

We show that the press conference correlates with future policy to a greater extent than other communications. While the FOMC statement coarsely signals the current stance of policy, the press conference fine-tunes the message, which helps market participants revise their expectations about future policy.

detail.abstract: This policy paper examines the prospects for a globally interconnected solar power transmission network by 2050, drawing on scenario planning methodology to map three plausible futures: a cooperative Global Solar Alliance driven by multilateral governance, an Energy Islands world fragmented by geopolitical protectionism, and a Global Energy Marketplace shaped by private investment and bilateral deals. Anchored along a notional Morocco-to-Australia transmission corridor and grounded in HVDC technology capabilities, the analysis identifies key inflection points technological, regulatory, and geopolitical that will determine which trajectory prevails. The paper concludes that a 24-hour global renewable energy grid is no longer a utopian vision but an actionable imperative, provided governments, businesses, and multilateral institutions act in concert without delay.

title: Building Epistemic Infrastructure for Enterprise AI Search: Why Retrieval Is Not Enough

detail.title: Building Epistemic Infrastructure for Enterprise AI Search: Why Retrieval Is Not Enough
detail.abstract: Enterprise adoption of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has exposed a critical bottleneck that transcends retrieval accuracy: epistemic fidelity. While current systems excel at semantic matching, they treat all retrieved knowledge as homogenous evidence, failing to distinguish between binding board decisions, abandoned hypotheses, contested claims, or unresolved organizational questions. This paper argues that the "knowledge-commitment gap" is the primary driver of the 95% failure rate in enterprise AI transformation. We critically examine the limitations of RAG and knowledge graphs, introduce the concept of Epistemic Infrastructure, and provide a rigorous analysis of the OIDA framework. We extend this work by proposing a Federated Epistemic Ledger (FEL) model and workflow-based epistemic decay. Finally, we outline a multi-dimensional evaluation methodology that moves beyond accuracy metrics to measure epistemic coherence.

detail.abstract:
In academic research environments, work that produces immediately observable and reviewable outputs tends to be prioritized over knowledge that requires time-dependent accumulation and process-based validation.
This paper documents a Recurring Capture Pattern (RCP) observed in academic evaluation systems centered on publications and peer review.
Under the institutional condition of static snapshot evaluation and single-point peer review that fixes evaluation at one moment in time, individually rational behavior systematically converges not toward long-term knowledge accumulation and value amplification but toward optimization of outputs that are observable and evaluable at a single point in time.
As these behaviors accumulate, they alter the evaluation structure itself, resulting in the progressive invisibilization of time-dependent and process-dependent knowledge and reinforcing the same behavioral convergence through a recursive institutional feedback loop.
The pattern ultimately produces an expansion of non-evaluable knowledge domains and structural fixation of time-non-extended evaluation axes, indicating a structural misalignment between institutional objectives and rational behavioral adaptation.
This paper analytically describes the structural relationship between institutional design and rational behavioral adaptation.

detail.title: Governance Friction Analysis of the Single-CEO Model under the National Environmental Protection Agency Act 2025
detail.abstract: The National Environmental Protection Agency Act 2025 replaces a board-based environmental regulator with a single Chief Executive Officer, consolidating nine regulatory functions within one Commonwealth entity and strengthening advisory and transparency mechanisms. Using the Governance Friction Analysis (GFA) framework, this paper evaluates how the single-CEO model balances decisional clarity, relational trust and systemic coherence across eight governance domains. Dynamic Lotka-Volterra simulations of relational trust (G₂), sectoral alignment (G₆), systemic coherence (G₇) and legitimacy (G₈) indicate that the model is structurally efficient yet relationally fragile, operating in a stable-frictional zone of governance vitality. While the NEPA Act 2025 enhances procedural pluralism through formal advisory committees, it does not introduce structural pluralism or resolve institutional dualism between the NEPA and EPBC regimes. The analysis identifies governance compression, pluralism deficit, delegation ambiguity and systemic drift as persistent friction types, and contends that long-term success depends on deliberate investment in relational infrastructure, policy coupling and reflexive oversight.

detail.abstract: This paper advances a governance-centered response to emerging critiques within quantitative research, particularly those articulated through Quantitative Critical Race Theory (QuantCrit). While QuantCrit provides a necessary critique of how statistical methods may reproduce systemic inequities, its proposals for corrective practice remain primarily methodological rather than architectural-offering tools for better research rather than structures for institutional accountability in algorithmic environments. This gap becomes consequential as artificial intelligence (AI) systems increasingly mediate educational decision-making, including assessment, placement, behavioral monitoring, and personalized learning pathways. Drawing from interdisciplinary foundations in Christian ethics, FAITH-BASED AI GOVERNANCE IN EDUCATION 2 educational theory, and AI governance, this paper introduces the Faithful Intelligence framework as a normative and operational model for ethical oversight in AI-driven educational systems. The framework integrates principles of stewardship, human dignity, and epistemic accountability with a Lean Six Sigmainformed ethical monitoring structure, proposing the Ethical Sigma Index (ESI) as a conceptual construct for detecting ethical deviations in algorithmic outputs alongside governance mechanisms-Ethical Review Gates and continuous institutional feedback loops. This paper argues that without structured ethical governance systems, critiques such as QuantCrit risk remaining intellectually influential but operationally insufficient against the scale and speed of algorithmic decision-making in contemporary educational environments.

title: Productive Hard Money Under Live Conditions: An Empirical Evaluation of the Algorithmically Stabilised Hard Asset Thesis Across Two Separate Protocol Deployments

detail.abstract:
Bindseil and Schaaf (2024) argue that non-productive hard assets generate price appreciation that is purely redistributive — gains to holders come at the expense of later entrants, with no net creation of economic value. The ASHA framework (Algorithmically Stabilised Hard Assets) proposes a class of protocol-based monetary assets that are hard in supply and productive in mechanism: endogenous token-denominated returns are generated by protocol-defined emission and share allocation, not by secondary market price appreciation. This paper presents the first empirical evaluation of the ASHA four-property thesis — hardness, predictability, productivity, and salability — using on-chain data from two separate live deployments: the Torus Protocol (Ethereum, genesis 2025-07-10, 268-day observation window) and the Unity Protocol (PulseChain, genesis 2025-08-18, 225-day observation window).

The analysis is based on 46 extracted datasets totalling approximately 370,000 on-chain event records. Three of the four ASHA properties are supported under observed live conditions. Hardness: BuyAndBurn achieved aggregate burn neutralisation rates of 43.74% (Torus, all governance periods) and 33.67% (Unity, full 225-day window), with governance responsiveness confirmed through the Torus period decomposition. Predictability: the difficulty curve adhered to its theoretical specification to within 0.001% relative error; governance parameter adjustments produced measurable, directionally predicted inflections in burn output. Productivity: 92.6% of completed Torus staking positions and 96.1% of Unity positions earned token-denominated rewards exceeding committed principal, with median reward ratios of 2.959x and 3.957x respectively — returns generated endogenously by the protocol mechanism, structurally distinct from the secondary-market price-appreciation channel that Bindseil and Schaaf (2024) characterise as redistributive. Whether token-denominated returns constitute macroeconomic productivity in the broader sense they discuss remains a question outside the scope of this Stage 1 analysis (see Section 8). Salability is partially supported: AMM liquidity venues operated continuously and the day-88 maturity cliff appeared independently on both protocols; the SMR incentive gradient produced Spearman correlations of 0.76 and 0.73 (p < 0.000001) between regime position and participant behaviour, but neither protocol recovered to the SMR within the observation window.

The most significant finding is behavioural convergence across separate deployments. Entry via Creation (89.2% versus 90.8%, χ2 = 0.985, p = 0.321), staking participation (51.3% versus 47.5%, χ2 = 1.912, p = 0.167), and median commitment duration (88 days on both protocols) did not differ significantly across two separate deployments on different blockchains with different reserve assets and a 39-day separation in genesis dates; deposit composition differs significantly between chains (Creation deposits χ2 = 29.74; combined Creation+Staking χ2 = 32.95; both p < 0.000001), consistent with chain-level native asset characteristics rather than architectural divergence. The replication is consistent with the ASHA mechanism generating similar behavioural structure under shared incentive architecture, although alternative explanations such as participant overlap and temporally proximate launches by a common designer cannot be excluded by this design. AEON — the structured research programme this paper initiates — is not a deployed system. It represents the next-stage research direction the empirical patterns suggest.

detail.abstract: In competition policy and antitrust litigation, the definition of 'cost' represents a contested terrain where legal outcomes frequently hinge on divergent accounting interpretations. While management accounting is able to provide a disciplined framework for internal control, it often fails to capture the dynamic economic realities of market power and strategic behaviour. By deconstructing the accountant's retrospective focus on historical cost recovery and the economist's forward-looking emphasis on marginalism and opportunity cost, the study analyzes the strategic role of endogenous sunk costs (Sutton, 1991), the arbitrariness of joint cost allocation (Kahn, 1970), and the limitations of the Areeda-Turner test (1975) to illustrate how traditional metrics can inadvertently veil predatory intent or mislabel lawful competition. The paper proposes a reconciliation centred on the adoption of Average Avoidable Cost (AAC) as a shared metric and the implementation of lifecycle-based 'Regulatory Management Accounting' standards, arguing for a diagnostic approach that prioritizes economic causality and interdisciplinary fluency to align internal organizational logic with the external objectives of market fairness and allocative e iciency.

title: The Architecture of Settlement

detail.title: The Architecture of Settlement
detail.abstract:
This paper examines the structural transformation of financial systems through the lens of settlement infrastructure. While the first wave of payments innovation focused on improving access, speed, and user experience, it left the underlying mechanisms of settlement largely unchanged. A new phase is now emerging-defined not by incremental optimization, but by a redesign of how value is transferred, recorded, and governed. 

The central argument is that the outcome of this transition depends not on technological capability alone, but on the governance choices that determine how these systems are structured, integrated, and scaled across jurisdictions. Settlement is becoming a core layer of system design-one that shapes how liquidity moves, how risks are managed, and how financial relationships are structured. 

The analysis identifies three converging developments shaping this transition: the rise of stablecoins as privately issued settlement assets, the development of central bank digital currencies (CBDCs) as public alternatives, and the expansion of tokenized financial assets that integrate payment and asset transfer. Together, these represent competing architectures for programmable financial infrastructure-each embedding different assumptions about control, interoperability, compliance, and the role of public versus private actors. 

The implications extend to financial institutions, asset managers, and policymakers, requiring new approaches to infrastructure participation, regulatory design, and strategic positioning.

title: Assessing the Validity of the Taxes and Levies (Approved List for Collection) Act, 1998 in the light of the Decision in A.G. Abia State v. Imo Trans. Co. Ltd. (2025) LPELR-80609(SC)

detail.title: Assessing the Validity of the Taxes and Levies (Approved List for Collection) Act, 1998 in the light of the Decision in A.G. Abia State v. Imo Trans. Co. Ltd. (2025) LPELR-80609(SC)
detail.abstract:
Due to multiple taxation ravaging Nigeria during the military era, the Military Government promulgated the Taxes and Levies (Approved List for Collection) Decree of 1998 (the “Decree”). The Decree was designed to set out the taxes and levies collectable by the three tiers of government: Federal Government (“FG”), State Government (“SG”) and Local Government (“LG”). The Decree became modified under section 315 of the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria (the “Constitution”) to the Taxes and Levies (Approved List for Collection) Act, 1998 (the “Act”). However, the validity of the Act continues to be a subject of constitutional criticism and judicial scrutiny as discernible from different Nigerian cases. The criticisms rest majorly on three (3) reasons which are: (i) arrogation of supremacy over the constitution to itself; (ii) housing unconstitutional provisions that offend the constitutional division of tax powers; and (iii) non-qualification of the Decree as existing statute.
In this article, we assessed the validity of the Act in the light of the recently decided case of AG Abia State v. Imo Trans. Co. Ltd (2025). We identified the criticisms levelled against the Act, reviewedrelevant Nigerian cases on the validity of the Act, and concluded thats by the decision in AG Abia State v. Imo Trans. Co. Ltd., the Act has become void and inoperative in Nigeria

detail.abstract: To understand how federal credit transmits through intermediaries, we study the Community Development Financial Institution (CDFI) program, which channels support through certification and competitive capital awards. We decompose participation into certification (eligibility), application (demand), and award receipt (allocation).  We show that these margins reflect distinct forms of selection. Certification is driven by persistent institutional characteristics, while application behavior among credit unions is associated with financial conditions. Conditional on application, award allocation is primarily related to profitability, indicating that while more constrained institutions seek funding, awards are directed toward those best positioned to deploy capital. Following award receipt, credit unions expand assets, lending, and non-deposit funding, while banks exhibit more limited responses. Certification also responds to anticipated local investment demand during the 2017 Opportunity Zone nomination phase. Our findings show that intermediary-targeted federal credit operates through distinct selection and allocation margins shaped by institutional form.

title: Accounting Alienation in Digital Capitalism: Platform Algorithms as Calculative Practices and the Colonization of Value Measurement

detail.title: Accounting Alienation in Digital Capitalism: Platform Algorithms as Calculative Practices and the Colonization of Value Measurement
detail.abstract: In the era of digital capitalism, platform algorithms have not merely automated existing accounting functions; they have fundamentally reconstituted the calculative logic through which costs, revenues, and value are defined. This study argues that accounting alienation in platform economies is, at its core, a crisis of calculative practice: algorithms displace the deliberative, relational foundations of accounting measurement, redefining what counts as labor, what constitutes a cost, and who bears accountability. Drawing on Peter Miller's framework of accounting as calculative practice, Marxist labor value theory, and surveillance capitalism, we examine how Meituan's algorithmic delivery system, deployed across approximately six million gig workers in China, operates as an invisible accountant: reconstituting labor time, externalizing occupational costs, and severing the face-to-face accountability relations that Roberts (1991) identifies as central to any legitimate accounting practice. Through granular analysis of Meituan's cost classification, data asset treatment, and ESG reporting, supported by comparative accounting tables, we demonstrate that the platform's reported financials systematically obscure a ￥3.3-4.8 billion annual gap between recognized rider costs and the full labor costs that an accountable system would require. The paper then offers a dialectically grounded critique of "digital labor accounting" reform: while necessary, extending calculative coverage to previously invisible labor risks, reinforcing the comprehensive commodification of human activity unless accompanied by structural accountability reform. This study enriches critical accounting theory by specifying the mechanism of algorithmic alienation rather than merely its existence. It provides regulators and practitioners with a concrete framework for evaluating platform labor disclosure.
