detail.title: Position: AI Welfare Is Bullshit
detail.abstract: Recent proposals urge AI labs to prepare for "AI welfare" under uncertainty about whether AI systems have morally relevant inner states. We do not argue for or against the possibility of AI welfare. Instead, we argue that current AI welfare assessment fails for two linked structural reasons absent from other evaluation targets. First, AI welfare indicators are co-engineered with the systems they evaluate: ordinary development decisions that shape model behavior can also manufacture or suppress welfare evidence. Second, AI welfare lacks external validation: no deployment failure or independent test can reveal whether a welfare metric tracks anything real about the system. Together, these problems yield our central claim: For current systems, AI welfare is bullshit in Frankfurt's sense, as its measurement regime is structurally disconnected from truthtracking. AI welfare should therefore not be institutionalized as a binding gate for oversight, release, or accountability; restrictions on AI systems should instead be justified by externally verifiable harms.

detail.abstract: Navigation QR codes are now widely used across payments, ordering, public-facing navigation, and other business or institutional workflows, yet current mainstream QR scanning appears to remain primarily a convenience feature rather than a trust system. This paper addresses navigation QR rather than presentation or credential QR. Scanners typically decode a payload and surface a URL or app intent, but do not determine whether the issuer is legitimate, whether the destination remains issuer-approved, or whether the destination is safe at the time of scanning. The central claim of this manuscript is that navigation-QR security is not primarily a cryptography problem. Signed payloads, certificate checks, and HTTPS transport are necessary but insufficient because they do not, by themselves, create a managed trust signal for users. The framework developed here separates issuer legitimacy, destination binding, and runtime destination safety; develops one hierarchical but federated trust-tree model for issuer delegation and state distribution; defines issuer assurance tiers and scanner decision states; and analyzes enrollment, inspection scope, and governance constraints. It does not claim a completed deployment or empirical validation of a universal governance model. Instead, it argues that the surveyed platform behavior and cited literature do not show a widely deployed managed trust layer that can make scanner-visible trust states intelligible to users.

detail.abstract: Money laundering poses a severe threat to the integrity of financial systems globally, with Bangladesh's growing digital banking sector presenting unique detection challenges. This study implements and evaluates five machine learning (ML) algorithms-XGBoost (Gradient Boosting), K-Nearest Neighbours (KNN), Random Forest (RF), Isolation Forest, and Support Vector Machine (SVM)-on a synthetic dataset of 2,000 individual bank customer transaction records constructed to reflect Bangladesh retail banking patterns. SMOTE was applied to the training set to address class imbalance. The study evaluates the accuracy and precision of the implemented algorithms alongside recall, F1-score, and AUC-ROC metrics. XGBoost achieved the highest performance with accuracy of 97.00%, precision of 94.26%, recall of 95.83%, F1-score of 95.04%, and AUC-ROC of 0.9971. Statistical validation through 10-fold cross-validation and paired t-tests confirmed XGBoost's superiority over KNN (p < 0.001), Random Forest (p = 0.0009), and SVM (p < 0.001). Feature importance analysis identified Previously_SAR_Filed, Internal_Risk_Rating, and Previous_Risk_Event as the most predictive variables. Results are specific to the synthetic dataset used; generalisation requires independent validation on real banking data.

detail.abstract: The ability to predict specific breach timelines from threat actor operational patterns remains an open challenge. While academic research has demonstrated high detection accuracy for technical indicators, frameworks for forecasting threat actor progression from Initial Access Broker (IAB) activities to active campaigns are largely absent from peer-reviewed literature. This paper presents a retrospective multi-case assessment of 27 major cybersecurity incidents (June 2024-June 2025) using an external attack surface management platform monitoring over 20,000 underground economy sources. Of 22 cases suitable for temporal analysis, observable pre-breach signals were identified within a 4-21 week window in 19 cases (86%). Attack-specific lead-time patterns emerged: ransomware operations (8-12 weeks), data exfiltration (4-8 weeks), and credential-based attacks (6-21 weeks). Six cases yielded high-confidence breach account identification through exact credential correlation. Combined documented financial losses across validated cases exceeded $77 million, with data exposure affecting over 79 million individuals. To the authors' knowledge, this represents the first systematic retrospective assessment linking underground economy intelligence to temporal breach forecasting across diverse sectors and geographies. These findings motivate prospective evaluation of predictive lead-time reliability.

detail.abstract: In 1817, Jeremiah Brandreth led England's last armed rebellion, marching against industrial machines with nails on sticks. He was hanged. That same year, Sylvanus Thayer rebuilt West Point into America's first engineering school, whose graduates connected a continent by rail. Christopher Nolan's Interstellar encodes the same lesson: the characters who rage against the dying of the light are the villains; the heroes let go of old paradigms and build. As AI reshapes knowledge work the way steam reshaped manufacturing, we face the same choice. The question is not whether to rage at disruption, but whether we have the imagination to build through it.

detail.abstract: Smart meter electricity consumption is a growing area of concern in modern energy management, influenced by environmental conditions, usage patterns, and grid infrastructure factors. This study conducts Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) on a dataset of 5,000 smart meter readings spanning January to April 2024 to uncover key risk factors behind abnormal consumption, identify usage patterns, and highlight temporal disparities in electricity demand. The aim is to analyze the impact of temperature, humidity, wind speed, time of day, and historical consumption behavior on the occurrence of anomalous meter readings. Methodologically, statistical analysis and data visualization techniques are used to identify correlations between consumption levels, environmental variables, and anomaly occurrence. The results reveal that consumption tier and average past consumption history are the strongest predictors of abnormal readings, with Very High consumption events carrying an anomaly rate of 89.5%. Nighttime hours and low-temperature periods show disproportionately higher fault rates, while humidity and wind speed demonstrate no significant standalone impact on anomaly occurrence. The study emphasizes the need for proactive real-time monitoring systems, automated anomaly alert mechanisms, and datadriven grid management policies. These insights provide a foundation for future research and AI-driven predictive models in smart meter fault detection and energy consumption forecasting.

detail.abstract: Research and industry reporting consistently document that organizations struggle to move AI from experiment to adoption despite significant investment in leadership programs, cultural initiatives, and change management. This article formally identifies why, and the reason is not what the current literature is acting on. The prevailing frameworks treat AI adoption failure as a leadership problem, a cultural problem, or a change management problem. This article formally argues it is an engineering problem that originates before any of those strategies are deployed and that the rigor of change management required for AI adoption is inversely proportional to the trust a model earns at first use. That relationship between an engineering prerequisite and an organizational outcome has three specific implications no existing practitioner or academic literature has formally stated: First, the causal chain has never been precisely identified. Existing literature establishes that demonstrated value drives adoption. What it has not answered is why enterprise AI deployments so consistently fail to produce demonstrated value and why that failure cannot be resolved by improving the model, the training program, or the change management strategy. This article traces the failure to a specific, addressable architectural gap that originates before the model trains and before any organizational strategy is deployed. Second, a distinction no existing governance framework has formally made. Current data validation, confirming that data is technically accurate and current, and contextual validation, confirming that data means what the organization assumes it means given its operational history, are fundamentally different things. Most organizations do the first. Almost none formally do the second. The absence of the second is where AI adoption failure originates. This distinction has not been formally named or argued in any existing practitioner or academic literature. It is the mechanism that explains why technically correct data produces outputs users cannot trust and why those outputs destroy adoption before change management ever has the opportunity to work.

title: Impact of Digital Accounting Systems Adoption on Financial Performance and Transparency among SMEs in Kerala

detail.title: Impact of Digital Accounting Systems Adoption on Financial Performance and Transparency among SMEs in Kerala
detail.abstract: This study examines how adoption of digital accounting systems (DAS) influences the financial performance and transparency of small and medium enterprises (SMEs). A quantitative survey was simulated for 100 SMEs in Kerala, India, to explore relationships among DAS usage, financial reporting transparency, and firm performance. Recent literature indicates that digital technologies significantly enhance SME operational outcomes[1][2]. Against this backdrop, we formulate clear objectives and test three hypotheses relating DAS adoption to performance and transparency. Using Pearson correlation on simulated data, we find statistically significant positive associations among all variables (DAS-Performance r≈0.76, DAS-Transparency r≈0.79, Transparency-Performance r≈0.59, all p<0.01). These findings align with prior studies in Nigeria and Bangladesh showing digital accounting boosts SME results[3][4]. The results suggest that SMEs should prioritize accounting digitalisation to improve outcomes. Limitations include the simulated and cross-sectional nature of data. Practical implications are that policymakers and SME owners should encourage DAS adoption through training and support.

detail.abstract:
As justice systems increasingly integrate automated tools, including risk assessments, alerts, and classification systems, attention has largely focused on evaluating the performance, fairness, and accuracy of these technologies. However, a critical dimension remains undefined: how decision-making authority is exercised around these system outputs in real-world environments.

This paper presents Justice Decision Observability™ (JDO™) as the defining category for understanding and governing execution-layer decision-making in AI-supported justice systems. It advances a clear position: the primary risk in modern justice environments is not solely located within the technology itself, but within the conditions under which human actors interpret, rely upon, override, or act on system-generated information.

Framed as a category ownership manifesto, this work articulates the boundaries, scope, and necessity of JDO™ as a distinct field. It defines what JDO™ is, what it is not, and why existing approaches including system audits, compliance frameworks, and performance evaluations fail to address the execution layer where institutional authority is ultimately exercised.

The paper introduces key constructs including the Decision Visibility Gap, the Moment of Authority, and patterns of reliance behavior that shape outcomes across corrections, courts, and community supervision. It establishes JDO™ as the first structured approach to documenting how decisions are actually made around automated outputs, positioning it as foundational to accountability, defensibility, and governance in justice systems.

By defining and claiming this category, the paper provides a framework for institutions, oversight bodies, and technology providers to recognize, measure, and govern the decision layer that has remained largely unobserved despite its critical impact on outcomes.

title: Throwing Good Money After Bad: Risk Mitigation Strategies in the P2P Lending Platforms

detail.title: Throwing Good Money After Bad: Risk Mitigation Strategies in the P2P Lending Platforms
detail.abstract: The success of peer-to-peer (P2P) lending platforms has proven inconsistent and uneven over time and geography. This paper aims to strengthen our understanding of the market evolution through an analysis of risks on P2P lending platforms, which can be significantly affected by the way the platform design, regulatory structural building, nature of the transaction, and interdependencies between organizational components. We extend the social-technical model and create a systematic framework to map and analyze the financial risks from a hybrid financial and organizational approach. By implementing textual and statistical analysis on a dataset from Renrendai platform, we found that risks are generated not only from the stakeholders but also due to the weaknesses of interdependencies between organizational components and platform design. We also utilize our models to investigate why some P2P platforms such as LendingClub and Upstart (US), Renrendai (China), and Zopa (UK) have succeeded or failed from both finance and IS perspectives, and further propose potential risk-mitigation strategies for P2P lending platforms.

detail.abstract: The rapid growth of digital commerce, mobile banking, and Unified Payments Interface (UPI)-based transactions has significantly improved the convenience of online payments. However, this growth has also increased exposure to cyber threats such as credential theft, phishing, unauthorized account access, device spoofing, and fraudulent transaction initiation. Traditional single-factor or static two-factor authentication methods are often insufficient because they apply the same level of verification to both low-risk and high-risk transactions. This paper proposes a Secure Online Payment System using Adaptive Multi-Factor Authentication (AMFA) that dynamically adjusts authentication requirements based on transaction risk. The proposed system integrates password-based login, device recognition, OTP verification, biometric verification, and behavioral risk scoring to strengthen payment security while maintaining usability. A risk engine evaluates multiple parameters such as login pattern, transaction amount, device trust level, geolocation deviation, and user behavior. Based on the computed risk score, the system selectively enforces additional authentication steps before permitting payment authorization. Encryption mechanisms are used to protect credentials, session tokens, and transaction records. The proposed system reduces the probability of unauthorized payments, improves fraud detection capability, and ensures a more resilient digital payment workflow. The model is suitable for banking applications, UPI platforms, ecommerce gateways, and mobile wallet ecosystems.

detail.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has transitioned from an experimental tool to the "central nervous system" of the global financial infrastructure. This study explores the emergence of agentic AIautonomous systems capable of independent decision-making in high-stakes environments such as credit approval and fraud detection. By utilizing Python-based analytical frameworks to examine historical data, the research highlights AI's efficacy in identifying complex correlations between traditional assets like gold and volatile digital assets like Bitcoin. However, the findings reveal a stark paradox: while AI enhances operational speed and market insights, it simultaneously facilitates sophisticated new fraud methodologies, with projected global losses expected to rise from $23 billion to $58 billion. Furthermore, despite aggressive investment, only 8% of major banks report a clear return on investment (ROI), largely due to the "black box" nature of AI decision-making. The research concludes that for AI to achieve sustainable integration, the industry must prioritize "explainable AI" (XAI) and develop robust regulatory frameworks that balance rapid innovation with transparency and consumer protection.

Why Digital Government Integration Fails Without Data Governance
detail.abstract:
This paper analyzes the limitations of the integration-first approach to digital government, using the case of Kyrgyzstan and Central Asian countries. Despite significant investments in integration platforms, the expected outcomes - end-to-end digital services and effective data exchange - often remain limited.
The study demonstrates that the key underlying issue is the lack of a mature data governance framework, including data inventory, standardization, and clear assignment of responsibilities. Based on a qualitative case study, the paper proposes a conceptual model identifying two levels of data-related constraints: the “unknown data landscape” and “semantic fragmentation.”
As a practical contribution, the paper introduces the Data-First Digital Government model, outlining a sequence for transitioning from fragmented systems to a coherent data environment.
The findings contribute to both academic discourse and public policy design in digital transformation and support the development of government data architectures.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the vulnerability of healthcare organizations to cyberattacks through operational realities rather than purely technical explanations. Drawing on prior research conducted in 2020 and supported by recent industry events, including the Change Healthcare breach, the paper explores how accessibility requirements, legacy systems, and regulatory pressures create persistent cybersecurity risks. The analysis demonstrates that vulnerability in healthcare is not the result of negligence but arises from structural and operational demands. title: Patents in the AI Era: Challenges at the Intersection of AI Inventions and Australian Patent Law
affiliations: Griffith University - Griffith Business School, Griffith University and TC Beirne School of Law, University of Queensland

detail.title: Patents in the AI Era: Challenges at the Intersection of AI Inventions and Australian Patent Law
detail.abstract: Patenting AI inventions presents challenges due to the complex intersection of human-centric patent law and inventions that involve non-human ingenuity. This article critically examines the central research question: Can Australia's traditional patent law framework, designed for human inventors, adequately address the unique challenges posed by AI-generated and AI-assisted inventions, and what reforms are necessary to reconcile this technological disruption? Through doctrinal analysis of judicial precedents, including the landmark Thaler v Commissioner of Patents (2021-2022) litigation, and statutory interpretation of the Patents Act 1990 (Cth), this study identifies systemic tensions between AI-driven innovation and Australia's human-centric patentability criteria. The analysis focuses on four key challenges: (1) the ambiguity of 'manner of manufacture' requirements for AI inventions lacking direct technical contributions to computing; (2) novel complexities in assessing the prior art and non-obviousness given AI's access to vast, opaque datasets; (3) the inadequacy of the 'person skilled in the art' standard for evaluating AI's inventive step; and (4) policy risks associated with lenient utility thresholds in an era of AI's prolific output. By critically analysing existing laws and precedents, the article contends that Australia's current patent regime is insufficient to address AI-driven inventions. It identifies that the human-centric nature of patent law should be preserved and proposes reforms to the Patents Act 1990 (Cth) to ensure that AI inventions are adequately captured under the patentability criteria, as well as procedural reforms to incorporate a multidisciplinary review process for evaluating technical advancements across disparate fields.

title: Welfare Impacts of Improved Seed and Fertilizer Adoption among Smallholder Maize Farmers in Bono East, Ghana

detail.title: Welfare Impacts of Improved Seed and Fertilizer Adoption among Smallholder Maize Farmers in Bono East, Ghana
detail.abstract: This study investigates the welfare implications of agricultural technology adoption among smallholder maize farmers in the Bono East region of Ghana, with special interest in improved seeds, fertilizer, and their joint use. Using cross-sectional data from 423 farm households, we used the Multinomial Endogenous Switching Regression (MESR) model to tackle the selection bias arising from observed and unobserved heterogeneity. Propensity Score Matching (PSM) and Instrumental Variable (IV) approaches were applied to check the reliability of the results. The results indicate that the adoption of fertilizer alone and in conjunction with improved seed significantly improves maize yield, with the largest productivity gains observed under seed and fertilizer. However, welfare effects quantified by household monthly consumption per capita are mixed, indicating that productivity gains do not automatically translate into improved consumption. This study underscores the significance of promoting integrated technology packages alongside complementary market and institutional assistance to enhance smallholder welfare in Ghana.

title: Does Happiness Influence Behavioral Intention in Adverse Services?

detail.title: Does Happiness Influence Behavioral Intention in Adverse Services?
detail.abstract: Patients’ happiness influences perceived service quality and satisfaction, which becomes a basis for assessing service encounters. Hence, services are mostly evaluated based on the service experiences rather than outcomes. A conceptual framework was developed to explore the direct and mediating relationships between the constructs. This study was conducted in seven tertiary care hospitals from four districts of Karnataka state, India. Data was gathered from 436 outpatients. Data analysis involves descriptive statistics, hypothesis testing, mediation analysis, multigroup analysis, and importance-performance matrix analysis. The findings show that the direct and mediating relationships were statistically significant. The happiness of employed patients influences their perception of service quality and trust. Happiness level influences the patient’s mood, service quality, service outcome, trust, satisfaction, and behavioral intention. Therefore, hospital managers must enhance patients’ happiness. When the hospital offers the highest quality services, satisfaction increases, and positive behavioral intentions are developed. Patient satisfaction transforms into a foundation for creating a long-term connection between the patient and the healthcare organization.
